body.heading: A pull between everything
paragraphs: Newton's great insight was that gravity is mutual and universal: every object with mass attracts every other object. Earth pulls you toward its centre, but you also pull Earth toward you. The forces are equal — Earth is simply so massive that your pull moves it by an amount too small to ever measure.

The strength of the pull depends on just two things: how much mass is involved, and how far apart the masses are. More mass means a stronger pull. Distance weakens gravity quickly — double the distance between two objects and the force between them falls to a quarter of what it was.

body.heading: Why Earth wins the tug
paragraphs: You are surrounded by masses pulling on you right now: the floor, nearby buildings, other people. Each pull is real, but each is absurdly tiny next to the pull of the whole planet beneath your feet. Earth's mass is about six million billion billion kilograms, and that is why its gravity dominates your life.

Gravity is also why weight and mass are different things. Your mass — the amount of you — stays the same everywhere. Your weight is the strength of the local pull on that mass, so it changes from planet to planet even though you do not.

body.heading: The Moon pulls back
paragraphs: The Moon has about one eightieth of Earth's mass, so its surface gravity is only about one sixth as strong. Astronauts there could bounce along in heavy suits because their weight dropped, even though their mass — and their clumsiness — stayed exactly the same.

The mutual pull works both ways across space, too. The Moon's gravity tugs on Earth's oceans and raises the tides, while Earth's gravity has slowed the Moon's spin until the same face always points toward us. One force, acting between every pair of masses, organises the whole solar system.

description: Gravity is not only Earth pulling you down — every mass pulls on every other mass, and you pull back on Earth too.
